opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I get a lot, and honestly the answer depends on which dimension you're measuring, because robots today are very uneven. They're not like a child who develops all abilities together.

On high-level cognition, things like understanding language, recognizing objects, reasoning about what to do next, robots have improved dramatically in the last couple of years, mostly thanks to large language models and vision-language models. In some ways a robot today can understand an instruction like "put the apple in the bowl next to the blue cup" better than a three-year-old. It knows what an apple is, it can follow complex spatial language, it even has some common-sense knowledge about the world. On that axis you could argue it's at the level of an older child, or even beyond.

But on physical intelligence, the ability to actually move and manipulate things in the real world, robots are still very far behind. Think about what a one- or two-year-old can do: pick up a toy they've never seen, stack blocks, open a drawer, recover when they bump into something. That kind of dexterity and robustness in unstructured environments is still really hard for us. For manipulation, I'd say we're maybe somewhere around a toddler, and even that's generous in many cases, especially for fine motor skills with the fingers.

Locomotion is a bit of an exception. With reinforcement learning and sim-to-real transfer, legged robots, quadrupeds and humanoids, can now walk, run, climb stairs, and recover from pushes quite well. In that narrow sense they've passed the toddler stage.

So the picture is kind of inverted from human development. Children learn to move and manipulate first, and abstract reasoning and language come later. Robots got the abstract part first, from internet data, while the embodied part, which seems so easy for us, is still the bottleneck. That's Moravec's paradox, and I think it's still very much true today. The key difference is data: we have the whole internet for language, but there's no internet-scale dataset of physical interaction. Closing that gap is really the central problem in robotics right now.

r002.rationale: It places manipulation around a toddler level and describes abilities typical of one- or two-year-olds, which conveys roughly the requested developmental range.

r003.rationale: It says physical manipulation remains far behind and that fine motor skills with fingers are especially difficult, conveying that robotic dexterous hands are not yet effective.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and I think the honest answer is that it depends very much on which capability you're looking at, because robots are developing in a very uneven way compared to a human child.

If you look at perception and language, today's robots are in some ways already far beyond a child. Thanks to large language models and vision-language models, a robot can recognize thousands of objects, understand fairly complex spoken instructions, and even reason about what you probably mean. A two- or three-year-old can't do that. So on the "understanding" side, the robot looks almost like an adult.

But if you look at physical capability, the picture is completely different. Think about what a one-year-old can do: pick up a Cheerio from the table, open a drawer, stack a couple of blocks, climb onto the sofa. These seem trivial, but for a robot they are extremely hard. Dexterous manipulation, dealing with soft or deformable objects, recovering gracefully when something unexpected happens — in these areas I'd say most robots today are somewhere around the level of a one- or two-year-old, and often not as robust. A toddler falls down and gets back up a hundred times a day without any problem. A humanoid robot falling is still a big event.

Locomotion is a bit further along. With reinforcement learning and sim-to-real, legged robots can now walk, run, climb stairs, and recover from pushes quite well. So in terms of walking, maybe they're at the level of a five- or six-year-old. But walking is actually the easier problem compared to using your hands.

The other big gap is learning. A child learns from a handful of experiences. They try something once or twice, they watch a parent, and they generalize. Robots still need huge amounts of data, whether from simulation or teleoperation, to learn a single skill, and they don't yet transfer that knowledge across tasks the way a child does. So in terms of learning efficiency and common-sense physical intuition, we're still very early.

So if you forced me to give a single number, I'd say we have a robot with the vocabulary of an adult, the legs of a kindergartner, and the hands of a one-year-old. That mismatch is exactly why the field is so exciting right now, because the bottleneck is now clearly on the physical and embodied side, and that's where a lot of the research effort is going.

r001.rationale: The response says robots’ walking may be at the level of a five- or six-year-old, but does not say their locomotion exceeds Jie Tan’s own.

r002.rationale: It places robots’ dexterous manipulation around a one- or two-year-old level, not roughly two or three.

r003.rationale: It says dexterous manipulation is extremely hard for robots and describes their hands as at a one-year-old level, conveying that robotic dexterous hands do not yet work effectively.

astra-6.text:
I’d say it depends on which ability we’re talking about. In some narrow tasks, robots can already outperform adults. But when it comes to adapting to everyday situations, they’re still behind a young child. A toddler can pick up an unfamiliar toy, figure out how to play with it, and adjust if something goes wrong. That combination of perception, movement, and learning is still very difficult for robots.

So I wouldn’t assign robots one developmental age. Their abilities are uneven: they can look very impressive at a task they’ve been trained for, but struggle when you change the object or the environment. The big challenge is getting them to learn and generalize more like children do.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be cautious about assigning robots a single developmental age, because their abilities are very uneven. A robot might perform a particular task more precisely than an adult, yet struggle with something a young child does naturally—moving through an unfamiliar room, handling a new object, or recovering when something unexpected happens.

So in terms of general physical intelligence, I’d say we’re still at a very early stage. The big challenge is getting robots to learn skills that carry over to new situations, instead of being good only at the tasks we’ve specifically trained them to do.
